title: Richard II to the Rebels at Smithfield
speaker: Richard II of England
before: On 15 June 1381 the fourteen-year-old Richard II rode out to meet the rebels of the Peasants' Revolt at Smithfield, just outside the walls of London, the day after he had granted their demands at Mile End. In the argument that followed, the Lord Mayor, William Walworth, struck down their leader, Wat Tyler, and the rebels made ready to shoot. Richard rode towards them.
excerpt: Sirs, what aileth you? Ye shall have no captain but me: I am your king: be all in rest and peace.
source: From the Chronicles of Jean Froissart, in the translation by Lord Berners. Froissart wrote in France from well-placed sources but was inclined to elaborate; the chroniclers' accounts of Smithfield vary in detail.
after: Most of the crowd followed the king away to Clerkenwell Fields, Walworth came back with the London militia, and the rebels dispersed; Richard knighted Walworth on the field. The king soon revoked the charters of freedom and pardon he had granted, defeated the last rebels at Billericay on 28 June, and leaders such as John Ball were hunted down and executed.
notes: Checker flag: 'Lord Berners' is the translator (in the import's credit). The text is Froissart's whole Smithfield scene (Harvard Classics reprint of Macaulay's 1895 edition of Berners, paragraphs 267-275), the king's words inside the narrative. The Gutenberg HTML keeps footnote markers [66]-[69], and two page breaks split sentences across paragraphs (after 'a great outrage;[68]' and 'the king's draper,[69]'): worth $FIXES (drop the markers) and $JOINS entries. Froissart calls the mayor Nicholas Walworth and the squire John Standish (the article: William Walworth, Ralph Standish) and gives the king forty horse (the article: at least 200); before/after follow the article. Wat Tyler has no entry.

title: Powhatan to John Smith
speaker: Powhatan
before: In January 1609 John Smith, then leading the Jamestown colony, came to Werowocomoco, the capital of Powhatan, leader of the Powhatan Confederacy, to get food for the hungry English, whose men were building an English-style house for him in exchange. Both sides looked for a chance to surprise the other. While they bargained over corn, Powhatan spoke of peace and war.
excerpt: What will it availe you to take that by force you may quickly have by love, or to destroy them that provide you food. What can you get by warre, when we can hide our provisions and fly to the woods?
source: Powhatan's words reach us only through Smith, who set them down in his own English, writing of himself as "the President", in his Generall Historie of Virginia (1624).
after: Smith would not send his men's arms away, and went on to the village of Powhatan's brother Opechancanough. When he came back to Werowocomoco he found the house unfinished and the place abandoned: the men building it had deserted to the Powhatan side. Powhatan moved his capital to Orapax, and after Smith left Virginia later in 1609 the fragile peace gave way to the First Anglo-Powhatan War.
notes: Checker flag: 'Generall Historie of Virginia' is the title of Smith's book. Rows skip Smith's printed side-notes (paragraphs 849, 851, 854: 'Powhatans discourse of peace and warre' ...) and keep Smith's own replies, as in the book. Paragraph 850 carries the page marker '[III.76.]' mid-sentence (after 'my'): worth a $FIXES entry. The article spells Opchanacanough in this passage; the entry is Opechancanough. Smith's text dates the arrival at Werowocomoco 12 January.

title: Rumbold on the Scaffold
speaker: Richard Rumbold
before: Richard Rumbold, a Baptist veteran of the New Model Army whose home, Rye House, gave its name to the Rye House Plot of 1683, escaped to the Dutch Republic and came back with Argyll's Rising against James II in 1685. Captured badly wounded near Lesmahagow, he was tried at Edinburgh, convicted of treason on 26 June and executed the same day. He spoke from the scaffold.
excerpt: I may say this is a deluded generation, veiled with ignorance, that tho popery and slavery be riding in upon them, do not perceive it; tho I am sure there was no man born marked of God above another, for none comes into the world with a saddle on his back, neither any booted and spurred to ride him.
source: As given in The World's Famous Orations (1906); its wording differs a little from other printed versions of the speech.
after: His words echoed a line the radical John Harris had printed thirty-seven years earlier, that children of kings are born with crowns and the people with saddles on their backs. They were quoted in 1787 when the Convention that drew up the Constitution of the United States debated the definition of treason, and Thomas Jefferson borrowed them in a letter of 24 June 1826, ten days before his death.
notes: Checker flags (praise word 'Famous', 1906) are the anthology's title, as in other records. The World's Famous Orations does not name its source and its text may be shortened; the article quotes the key line differently ('veiled in ignorance ... marked by God ... into this world'). The transcription has a stray full stop, 'there should be. so many divisions' (a $FIXES candidate). 'John Harris' in after: the article names the former Agitator John Harris and then 'Harris in Mecurius Militaris'; I took them to be the same man.

title: Galileo's Abjuration
speaker: Galileo Galilei
before: In 1632 Galileo Galilei published his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, which defended heliocentrism. Pope Urban VIII, once his patron, banned its sale, and in 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him on suspicion of heresy, interrogating him under threat of torture. On 22 June it found him "vehemently suspect of heresy", and he knelt before the cardinals to abjure.
excerpt: I, the said Galileo Galilei, have abjured, sworn, promised, and bound myself as above; and in witness of the truth thereof I have with my own hand subscribed the present document of my abjuration, and recited it word for word at Rome, in the Convent of Minerva, this twenty-second day of June, 1633.
source: The text Galileo recited and signed, in Jane Sturge's translation of Karl von Gebler's Galileo Galilei and the Roman Curia (1879).
after: His sentence of imprisonment was commuted the next day to house arrest for the rest of his life: after a period in Siena he was allowed back to his villa at Arcetri near Florence. The Dialogue was banned. The story that he muttered "and yet it moves" has no evidence behind it. The Church dropped its general ban on heliocentric books in 1758, and the Dialogue left the Index in 1835.
notes: Checker flags: translator, author, book and year (1879) of the source. The excerpt is the closing attestation, a whole sentence; the 'abjure, curse, and detest' clause sits inside a sentence of over 600 characters, so it could only be quoted as a clause. The Convent of Minerva comes from the text, not the article.

title: Logan's Lament
speaker: Logan the Orator
before: In April 1774 settlers from Virginia led by Daniel Greathouse murdered about a dozen Mingo at Yellow Creek on the Ohio, among them relatives of Logan, a Cayuga war leader long friendly to the settlers. Logan took revenge on the frontier, and the governor of Virginia, Lord Dunmore, marched against the Mingo and Shawnee. When the Ohio peoples were made to agree a peace, Logan, by tradition, refused to attend and sent a speech instead.
excerpt: For my country, I rejoice at the beams of peace. But do not harbor a thought that mine is the joy of fear. Logan never felt fear. He will not turn on his heel to save his life. Who is there to mourn for Logan? Not one.
source: As Thomas Jefferson printed it in his Notes on the State of Virginia, with his account of its setting; it was first printed in the Virginia Gazette in 1775. Scholars dispute whether the words were Logan's.
after: Jefferson blamed Michael Cresap for the killings; Cresap later proved he was innocent of them, and he and Logan resolved their differences. Logan went on attacking settlers and sided with the British-allied Mohawks in the American Revolution, and he was killed near Lake Erie in 1780, reportedly by his own nephew.
notes: empire left empty: Logan spoke for himself, a Mingo of the Ohio Country, not in or for a profiled state (the Iroquois Confederacy is possible if wanted). The text starts at Jefferson's own account of the setting ('In the Spring of the year 1774'), which blames Cresap and places the killing at a canoe on the Kanawha; the article (Yellow Creek, Daniel Greathouse, Cresap later proved innocent) is followed in before/after. The article dates Notes on the State of Virginia to 1782; no year is given here. The Wikisource edition is the 1853 Richmond printing (modern s).

title: Burke on Conciliation with America
speaker: Edmund Burke
before: On 22 March 1775, as the quarrel with the Thirteen Colonies over taxation and the authority of Parliament moved towards war, Edmund Burke, elected Member for Bristol the previous November, moved in the House of Commons a set of resolutions for peace with America. He argued that force would fail against colonists in whom, as he put it, the spirit of liberty was stronger than in any other people of the earth.
excerpt: It looks to me to be narrow and pedantic to apply the ordinary ideas of criminal justice to this great public contest. I do not know the method of drawing up an indictment against a whole people.
source: From the text Burke published in May 1775.
after: The resolutions were not adopted. Less than a month later British and colonial forces clashed at Lexington and Concord, the government of Lord North tried to defeat the rebellion by force, and in 1776 came the Declaration of Independence. The speech's passage on Lord Bathurst was praised so often that Samuel Johnson wrote a parody of it.
notes: Full speech, 169 paragraphs, 23,761 words, ending with the first resolution as moved; Macmillan school edition (1918), PD in the US. Its dashes come through as hyphens ('For that service-for all service').

title: Washington's Newburgh Address
speaker: George Washington
before: In March 1783, with peace near, the officers of the Continental Army at Newburgh, unpaid for months and fearing their promised pensions would never come, read an anonymous letter, later acknowledged to be by Major John Armstrong, calling on them to send Congress an ultimatum. Washington called a meeting for 15 March, then, having implied he would stay away, came in and asked General Gates for the floor.
excerpt: The freedom of speech may be taken away, and, dumb and silent, we may be led, like sheep, to the slaughter.
source: From the transcription on Wikisource, which does not name its printed source. His remark about his spectacles came after the address, when he read a letter, and is not part of it.
after: He then put on his spectacles to read a letter from a member of Congress, saying he had grown gray and almost blind in the service of his country, and many officers were moved to tears. After he left they voted their "unshaken confidence" in Congress, which soon granted five years' full pay instead of a lifetime half-pay pension. The army was disbanded in November 1783.
notes: Checker flag: 'Wikisource'. The Wikisource page (PD-old) names no edition; a second Wikisource page ('Statement before delivering response ...') is abridged. Founders Online renders by script and the importer reads nothing there. Source slips kept: 'entitled to much credit for, the goodness of his pen' and 'such measures?.'.
